overview:
By the spring of 1948 two national movements had been contesting the same small territory for three decades. Britain had governed Palestine under a League of Nations mandate since the First World War, committed on paper both to a Jewish national home and to the rights of the Arab majority already living there, and by 1947 it wanted out. In November of that year the UN General Assembly voted to partition the territory into Jewish and Arab states with Jerusalem internationally administered; Zionist leaders accepted, Palestinian Arab leaders and the Arab League rejected it, and a civil war broke out at once between the two communities. When the last British forces left and Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, armies from Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq crossed into the former mandate the following day. The fighting ran, through two UN truces, into 1949 and ended not in peace treaties but in four separate armistices signed on Rhodes. Israel held roughly a fifth more land than the partition plan had allotted it; Egypt was left administering Gaza and Transjordan the West Bank and East Jerusalem. Those armistice lines, the Green Line, held until 1967. Somewhere around 700,000 Palestinians — the figure is contested, and how many fled and how many were expelled is contested harder — lost their homes, an event remembered as the Nakba, the catastrophe, and as the War of Independence on the other side of the same line. In the years that followed, most Jewish communities across the Arab world and Iran also left or were driven out.

What began as a war over one territory hardened into a regional confrontation, and it changed shape roughly every decade. Full interstate wars came in 1956 over Suez, in 1967, and in 1973; between them lay the grinding artillery duel along the canal that Egypt called the War of Attrition, running from 1969 into 1970. But much of the conflict was never fought by armies facing each other. It was fought at airports and embassies and across borders by raid — Palestinian gunmen attacking an El Al airliner at Athens in 1968, the hijacking of Sabena Flight 571 to Lod in 1972, Israeli long-range strikes on Iraq's Osirak reactor in 1981 and on PLO headquarters outside Tunis in 1985, an unacknowledged bombing of a suspected Syrian reactor in 2007, ground operations in Gaza such as Rainbow and Days of Penitence in 2004, and repeated strikes on Iranian-linked targets in Syria from 2018 onward. The Cold War overlaid all of it: Soviet arms and advisers on one side, American backing on the other, and in 1973 a nuclear alert on both.

The state-versus-state version of the conflict has largely wound down. Egypt made peace in 1979 and recovered Sinai, Jordan followed in 1994, the Oslo Accords created a Palestinian Authority without resolving what it would govern, and the Abraham Accords of 2020 normalised Israel's relations with the UAE, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan. What did not end was the unresolved core: the status of the territories occupied in 1967, the refugees of 1948 and their descendants, and the rise of armed non-state movements — the PLO, then Hamas and Hezbollah — backed increasingly by Iran rather than by Arab capitals. The war that began in October 2023 in Gaza is the most destructive chapter of that later phase.
significance: The 1948 war set the political geography of the modern Middle East and created two of its most durable facts: a Jewish state that has never had settled borders, and a Palestinian refugee population that now numbers in the millions and has its own permanent UN agency. It made the Middle East a standing arena of superpower competition and later of American diplomacy, drove the oil embargo of 1973 that reshaped the world economy, and produced the templates for much of what followed — preventive strikes on nuclear programmes, aircraft hijacking as political leverage, targeted killing across sovereign borders. Almost eighty years on, the questions the armistice lines of 1949 deliberately left open are still the ones being fought over.
coverage: Written from Britannica and Wikipedia overviews, the US State Department's Office of the Historian account of 1948–49, and UN material on the Nakba; the dataset itself is a poor guide to this story, holding nine events that all fall between 1968 and 2018 — mostly Israeli military operations and aircraft attacks — with nothing from 1948 and none of the major wars except the War of Attrition, and nothing on diplomacy, occupation or civilian experience. The wider record is unevenly open: Israeli archives were partially declassified from the 1980s and drove a real historiographical reckoning over expulsion in 1948, while Arab state and Palestinian records are far less accessible, and casualty, refugee and displacement figures remain disputed along political lines rather than settled by evidence.
